extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent examiners, inventors/R&D managers, SPL (substantive patent law) experts, and patent litigators focused on emerging/model-based technologies
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether an emerging/model‑based claimed invention (ETCI) satisfies substantive patent law (SPL) under the Supreme Court's Mayo/Bilski/Myriad/Alice (MBA) framework by (1) identifying inventive concepts and (2) applying a procedural FSTP test (nine subtests) to produce a refined claim interpretation and construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of determining inventive concept(s) (inC(s))
rubrics_metrics.description: The MBA framework (as applied in Enfish & TLI) requires first determining an ETCI's 'inventive concept(s), inC(s)' as the foundational basis for enabling correct and complete description of the ETCI within SPL testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper treats inC(s) as indispensable: enabling refined claim interpretation and construction, enforcing 'levels of abstraction', and forming the proper semantic/pragmatic basis for all subsequent SPL tests. Enfish and TLI are cited as acknowledging this necessity; the author argues that testing should start with extracting inC(s) from the specification as understood by the person of pertinent ordinary skill and creativity (pposc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels of abstraction must be determinable from inC(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ETCI's applicable 'levels of abstraction' must be determined by its inC(s) so that the invention's representations (O-/A-/E-levels) are properly aligned for SPL analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MBA framework implies and Enfish confirms that levels of abstraction are enforced by the inC(s). These levels separate O-level (ordinary descriptions) from A-/E-level refined knowledge representations used by the FSTP test; they are essential to avoid speculative/metaphysical reasoning and to enable rationalized (potentially automatic) testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation must depend on inC(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: A correct claim interpretation for an ETCI should be founded on the invention's inC(s) rather than solely on a literal list of claim limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper cites Enfish (page references) asserting the claim interpretation step must be grounded in the inC(s), enabling a refined (context-sensitive) interpretation that supports rational SPL testing rather than free‑style or purely limitations‑based interpretation (criticized as BRIPTO-style).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction must depend on inC(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction (the court/examiner's formal construing of claim scope) should follow from the inC(s) (and the resulting claim interpretation) to ensure determinate, MBA-consistent outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author frames claim construction as the final step of a 2-step algorithm (inC(s) → claim interpretation → claim construction) required by the MBA framework and reflected in Enfish/TLI; proper construction may obviate certain speculative pitfalls and aligns with refined procedural testing (FSTP).

rubrics_metrics.name: FSTP-Test (Facts Screening/Transforming/Presenting) — procedural, rational refinement of the TS test
rubrics_metrics.description: FSTP is proposed as a procedural, exhaustive, and rational refinement of the Supreme Court's Two‑Step (TS) test for subject‑matter eligibility; it operates mainly at A-/E-levels (refined knowledge representations) and is intended to be (largely) automatable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper states three claims about FSTP: (I) it is a rational refinement of the TS test; (II) an exhaustive refinement; (III) the only rational exhaustive refinement. FSTP moves from O-level descriptions (TS) to A-/E-level refined representations and enables deterministic/rational argumentation and potential automation. Passing the FSTP-Test (all component tests) indicates alignment with the MBA framework. The paper includes a formalized Figure 2 and claims executability even fully automatically where Rational (otherwise semi-automatic).

rubrics_metrics.name: FSTP test 1 — Biosig-test (novelty/definiteness/completeness requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Biosig-test is passed iff the examined COM(ETCI#) describes a new and useful invention and the COM(ETCI#) is definite and complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper links this test to ensuring the claimed invention (as represented by the COM construct) meets basic patentability prerequisites (new/useful) and that the communication/representation is definite and complete. Failing this test indicates absence of an inventive concept or insufficient disclosure for rational testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: FSTP test 2 — ETCI Disclosure-test (lawful disclosure / implementability disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: ETCI Disclosure-test is passed iff every element (∀ϵ) of COM(ETCI#) is lawfully disclosed (COM(ETCI#) ⇒ COM(ETCI)) and, for all A‑crC elements, implementability is disclosed 'for being E‑crC tested'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This test checks that the specification lawfully and adequately discloses the components and that disclosed actionable/implementable components are available to be tested at the E-level. It underpins the possibility of conducting the remaining FSTP subtests meaningfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: FSTP test 3 — ETCI Enabling-test (existence of implementable E-crC)
rubrics_metrics.description: ETCI Enabling-test is passed iff E‑crC \ E‑crCmod(A*#) ≠ ∅ (i.e., there is at least one implementable E‑crC after considering modifications for the asserted application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formal condition captures enablement: the specification must enable at least one implementable embodiment/element so that E‑level testing can proceed. If no implementable E‑crC exists, the ETCI cannot be rationally tested for SPL satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: FSTP test 4 — Bilski-test (identifiability of unlimitedly preemptive E-crC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bilski-test is passed iff the set ULPE‑crC (the set of E‑crC elements that are unlimitedly preemptive) is identifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This test seeks to identify any elements of the claimed invention that would afford unlimited preemption (which Bilski and related doctrine caution against). If such unlimitedly preemptive elements exist and cannot be identified/mitigated, patent-eligibility may fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: FSTP test 5 — Mayo/Myriad/Alice-related test (statutory exceptions / abstractness / natural law checks)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mayo-/Myriad-test (and the Alice-test as incorporated) is passed iff the combined subtests (including Alice-related subtests 1–5 as used in the paper) hold and there is no E‑crC outside ULPE‑crC that is unlimitedly preemptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This composite test operationalizes the Supreme Court's Mayo/Alice/Myriad analytical concerns within the FSTP framework: determine whether claimed subject matter is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon), and if so, whether the claim applies that exception in a way that transforms it into patent‑eligible subject matter. The paper treats this as an explicit FSTP condition (see Figure 2 and associated text).

rubrics_metrics.name: FSTP test 6 — (Numbering indicates tests 1–9; tests 6–9) Independence-test
rubrics_metrics.description: Independence-test is passed iff all E‑crC0nk (for all n,k) are independent of each other (i.e., no element is functionally dependent on another in a way that undermines inventive contribution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper formalizes independence via ANM predicates (if two E‑crC elements are equal within tolerances then marked 'A' else 'N'); independence supports separating inventive increments and avoids conflating elements such that inventive concepts become indeterminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: FSTP test 7 — KSR(RS)-test (obviousness / rationale test)
rubrics_metrics.description: KSR(RS)-test (obviousness-related) is applied across enumerated element indices (formalized in the paper) as part of assessing inventive step (reasoned-synthesis or RS analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although only tersely formalized in the text, this test corresponds to KSR/Graham obviousness analysis performed at the refined knowledge levels (RS), integrated into the FSTP sequence to check whether claimed combinations are obvious in light of the relevant refined records.

rubrics_metrics.name: FSTP test 8 — Graham(RS)-test (Graham factors applied at RS level)
rubrics_metrics.description: Graham(RS)-test is passed iff the vector <∀nk ϵ = A> is not a member of the set {∀AC over ANM} (formalized criterion indicating that the aggregated ANM status does not show lack of inventive contribution under Graham factors at the RS level).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalized test operationalizes the Graham factors (secondary considerations, scope/contents of prior art, differences, level of ordinary skill) at the refinedrepresentation level, using the ANM matrix to determine whether the assertion of obviousness holds; the paper provides a formal predicate-based guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the Supreme Court's Two‑Step (TS) test as an 'outer shell' — supplement with FSTP for content
rubrics_metrics.description: The TS test is characterized as declarative/non‑procedural and largely O‑level (speculative metaphysics) and thus insufficient for rational, determinate ETCI testing; it should be supplemented (content filled in) by the procedural FSTP test operating at A-/E‑levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper quotes Justice Breyer's 'outer shell' metaphor and argues that the Supreme Court intended experts/courts to 'fill in' the TS test's content. The FSTP test is presented as the way to fill that shell systematically and to eliminate the indeterminacy associated with TS-only approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use USPTO EPQI / MRF / IES to disseminate and operationalize MBA-based tests
rubrics_metrics.description: MRF‑based communications (Master Review Form within USPTO's Enhanced Patent Quality Initiative) and an Innovation Expert System (IES) should guide users first through classical claim interpretation & construction and then automatically into the MBA‑framework refined claim interpretation & construction (FSTP-guided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper recommends integrating FSTP/IES with USPTO EPQI (MRF) so examiners, applicants, and stakeholders are guided context‑sensitively through Q/A, classical tests, and then the procedural MBA/FSTP refinement, enabling widespread, efficient, and consistent application of the MBA framework when evaluating ETCIs. It emphasizes stepwise user guidance, peer Q/A, and potential automation to improve patent quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refined claim interpretation vs. refined claim construction separation (operational guide)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the FSTP framework, refined claim interpretation (above the dashed line) is separated from refined claim construction (below the line); depending on result (e.g., RS = ∅) certain tests (notably tests 4–8) may be skipped for claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure legend explains that the horizontal dashed line separates refined claim interpretation from claim construction and that the latter can, in some cases, skip several FSTP subtests. This provides operational guidance about the sequencing of refinement and which subtests apply at which stage.
